questions.prompt: Which code shape is usually described as O(1) average-case query work?

options.label: Scanning an unsorted array until a match appears.
Checking membership in a prebuilt hash set.
Comparing every item with every other item.

questions.explanation: A hash set lookup is usually flat average-case query work after the set has been built.

questions.prompt: Fill the gap for a function that does n^2 pair checks and then one linear cleanup pass.
questions.template: The simplified Big O time is {{blank}}.
questions.explanation: The quadratic pair checks dominate the later linear pass as input grows.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning for replacing repeated list scans with a set.

items.label: Notice that the membership check repeats.
Build a set once from the lookup values.
Call out the extra O(n) memory.

questions.explanation: A strong explanation says why the repeated query exists, where setup work moved, and what memory was added.

questions.prompt: Match each code shape to its usual Big O label.

pairs.prompt: Halve the remaining sorted range each step
Compare each item with many other items

questions.explanation: Big O follows the execution shape: halving is logarithmic, one pass is linear, and pairwise comparison is quadratic.

questions.prompt: What tradeoff does the standard hash-map Two Sum solution make?

options.label: It uses less memory to keep the same O(n^2) runtime.
It uses O(n) extra space to reduce time to O(n).
It sorts the array and keeps original indices for free.

questions.explanation: The map stores previous values so each new value can be checked once, trading memory for time.

questions.prompt: Why do graph algorithms often use V and E instead of only n?

options.label: Nodes and edges can grow independently, so both dimensions matter.
Graph algorithms are always O(1) after setup.
V and E hide the memory cost of the algorithm.

questions.explanation: A graph with the same number of nodes can have very different numbers of edges, so traversal cost often names both.
